messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content: Let (M,d) be a metric space. Does every Cauchy sequence in M have a limit in M? If (F_n) satisfies the stated hypotheses, choose x_n in F_n. For m <= n with m,n large, d(x_m,x_n) <= diam F_m, so (x_n) is Cauchy. Which limit does this Cauchy sequence have? Completeness gives a limit x, and each closed F_n contains the tail x_k (k >= n), so x lies in every F_n. Therefore the intersection of all F_n is nonempty. Why would the reverse implication hold? Given a Cauchy sequence (x_n) in M, define F_n = closure of {x_k : k >= n}. Their diameters tend to 0 because (x_n) is Cauchy. Does the assumed intersection property then force a limit? A point in every F_n lies within diam F_n of every tail point, so it is the limit of (x_n) and M is complete.
